claims.text: Tar is a sticky mixture of particles in tobacco smoke that condenses on the lining of the airways and alveoli. Many of the chemicals in tar are carcinogens, substances that can cause cancer. Tar and its carcinogens are separate from nicotine and carbon monoxide, which pass into the blood.

Syllabus wording and biology differ slightly: the syllabus lists tar and carcinogens side by side, but in standard biology the carcinogens of tobacco smoke are largely carried in the tar, so they are taught together here and tar is not treated as a second, separate cause of cancer.

claims.text: Carcinogens from tar reach the epithelial cells lining the bronchi and can damage their DNA, causing mutations. A mutation in a gene that controls cell division may let the cell divide out of control, and over years of smoking further mutations build up, so a tumour forms. The tumour can block a bronchus, destroy lung tissue and reduce the surface area for gas exchange, and cells that break away can start tumours elsewhere.

claims.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a long-term disease in which airflow is obstructed and the damage is not fully reversible; it includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema. In chronic bronchitis, tar and other irritants paralyse and then destroy the cilia, goblet cells enlarge and make more mucus, the mucus is not swept out and collects in the airways, the smoker coughs persistently, bacteria multiply so infection and inflammation follow, and the narrowed airways restrict airflow.

Syllabus wording and biology differ slightly: the syllabus attributes COPD to tar; in standard biology COPD results from the irritants in smoke as a whole (tar, other particles and gases) acting over years, so the claim says tar and other irritants. Asthma is a separate condition and is not part of COPD.

claims.text: In emphysema, tar and other irritants in smoke inflame the lung tissue and white blood cells collect there and release the enzyme elastase, which digests the elastic fibres in the alveolar walls. The alveoli lose their elastic recoil, so air is trapped on breathing out, and their walls break down so that neighbouring alveoli merge into fewer, larger air spaces with a smaller total surface area for gas exchange; less oxygen diffuses into the blood and the person is breathless.

claims.text: Within minutes of smoking, nicotine stimulates the nervous system so that the heart rate increases, and it narrows the small arteries (arterioles), which raises blood pressure. Nicotine also tends to make platelets stickier, which raises the chance that a blood clot forms. These effects last for minutes to hours, so they are short-term effects.

Heart rate and blood pressure effects are well established. The effect on platelet stickiness is stated in many teaching sources but the evidence is less consistent, so it is written as a tendency and left unverified.
The body's nervous and hormonal control of the heart is outside this syllabus, so the mechanism is given only as nicotine stimulating the nervous system.

claims.text: Carbon monoxide, formed when tobacco burns with too little oxygen, diffuses across the alveolar wall into red blood cells. Haemoglobin has a much higher affinity for carbon monoxide than for oxygen, more than 200 times its affinity for oxygen, so carbon monoxide binds to the haem iron to form stable carboxyhaemoglobin and oxygen is outcompeted. The syllabus describes this as carbon monoxide reducing the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. Less haemoglobin is available to carry oxygen, so each litre of blood carries less oxygen and the tissues, including the heart muscle, receive less oxygen.

claims.text: Together, nicotine and carbon monoxide leave the heart working harder while its own oxygen supply falls: nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure, and carbon monoxide lowers the oxygen content of the blood so the heart tends to beat faster to deliver more blood. Damage to artery walls over years is a longer-term effect.

Syllabus wording and biology differ slightly: the syllabus says incidence, which strictly means new cases in a stated period. A questionnaire that asks about new diagnoses in a stated period measures incidence; one that asks who currently has or has ever had the condition measures prevalence, the proportion affected. The notes teach the distinction and word the questionnaire for new diagnoses in twelve months.

claims.text: A survey result describes the sample, and it is a good estimate of the population only if the sample was chosen at random and is large enough. Answers are self-reported and may be inaccurate, hay fever is seasonal so the time of year of the survey affects the result, and a difference between two groups shows an association but does not show its cause.
